content: All concerns or comments can be submitted anonymously. If any content you have contributed is found to be plagiarized from another source, you will be removed as an editor from the page. What is Plagiarism? Plagiarism is the act of using someone else’s words or ideas without giving proper credit. Even if you make minor changes to the text and cite the source, you may still be guilty of plagiarism. Whether intentional or unintentional, plagiarism is a serious issue that can have legal consequences. How Can Plagiarism Be Avoided? Always cite your sources. If a source is copyrighted, you must summarize the content in your own words in addition to citing the source. For copyleft sources, you may copy content directly as long as you cite the source. However, be aware that the original poster of the content on a copyleft source may have plagiarized it from another source. Create content using original words and sentence structures. Simply changing a few words in a sentence may not be sufficient to avoid a claim of plagiarism. Use search engines to verify whether the material you have was taken directly from another source. When in doubt, ask. Contact us with any questions regarding plagiarism or the principles of copyleft and copyright. If you see any content on WikiDoc that you believe violates copyright or constitutes plagiarism, please let us know. Also, refer to WikiDoc’s disclaimers. Guidelines for Avoiding Plagiarism The following guidelines are adapted from Avoiding plagiarism, self-plagiarism, and other questionable writing practices: A guide to ethical writing by Miquel Roig: 1. Ethical writers always acknowledge the contributions of others and the sources of their ideas. 2. Any verbatim text taken from another author must be enclosed in quotation marks. 3. Always acknowledge every source used in your writing, whether you paraphrase, summarize, or quote it. 4. When summarizing, condense a substantial amount of material into a short paragraph or sentence using your own words. 5. Whether paraphrasing or summarizing, always identify the source of the information. 6. When paraphrasing or summarizing others’ work, ensure you reproduce the exact meaning of the original ideas or facts using your own words and sentence structure. 7. To create a proper paraphrase, you must thoroughly understand the ideas and terminology being used. 8. Ethical writers have a responsibility to respect others’ ideas and words, credit those from whom they borrow, and use their own words whenever possible. 9. When unsure whether a concept or fact is common knowledge, provide a citation. 10. Authors submitting manuscripts for publication must clearly indicate any prior dissemination of the data, reviews, or conclusions (e.g., in another journal, at a conference, or online). 11. Authors of complex studies should present results cohesively in a single paper rather than fragmenting them into multiple papers. If there is doubt about fragmented data, authors should include related papers for consideration. 12. Extensive paraphrasing or quoting of key elements of a book can constitute copyright infringement. Authors are encouraged to familiarize themselves with copyright law. 13. Text recycling may be acceptable in some situations but not in others. Authors should use proper paraphrasing and quotation practices. 14. Authors should double-check their citations to ensure accuracy and correspondence between in-text references and the reference list. 15. References in a paper should only include those directly related to its content. Including irrelevant references to manipulate impact factors or acceptance chances is unethical. 16. Strive to obtain the actual published paper. If unavailable, cite the specific version of the material used (e.g., conference presentation, abstract, or unpublished manuscript). 17. Avoid relying on secondary summaries of others’ work. Always consult the primary literature to ensure accuracy and scholarly integrity. 18. Clearly indicate the source of information being reported, especially when borrowing heavily from a source. 19. When appropriate, report evidence that contradicts your point of view and ensure supporting evidence is methodologically sound. Highlight any flaws in supporting studies. 20. Authors have an ethical obligation to report all aspects of a study that may impact the independent replicability of their research. 21. Researchers must report results according to their a priori plans. Any post hoc manipulations, such as eliminating outliers or using alternative statistical techniques, must be clearly described with a rationale. 22. Authorship determination should be discussed before starting a research collaboration and should follow established guidelines, such as those of the International Committee of Medical Journal Editors. 23. Only individuals who have made substantive contributions to a project merit authorship in a paper. 24. Faculty-student collaborations should follow the same criteria for authorship. Mentors must ensure authorship is neither unfairly awarded nor denied to students. 25. Academic or professional ghost authorship in the sciences is ethically unacceptable. What Does Copyleft Mean? Copyleft is a principle that allows information to be freely copied, modified, or redistributed, provided that: The new version grants the same freedoms to others. The original authors of the content are acknowledged. You can copy and paste directly from copyleft material as long as your work adheres to these two rules. Where Can I Find Copyleft Material? Copyleft material can often be found under Creative Commons licenses or similar principles. However, one exception is the National Guidelines Clearinghouse, where the copyright of the original society or entity must be respected. Large sections of background materials from such guidelines should not be distributed without permission. What About Other Websites or Journal Articles That Are Copyrighted? If a source is copyrighted, you are legally prohibited from copying it without permission. Simply changing or adding a few words does not absolve you of the act of stealing someone else’s words and ideas.
